column5: fire and worms felt forever in the flesh
column6: Judith's final hymn says that God will put fire and worms into the flesh of hostile nations and that they will feel them forever; its enduring bodily sensation is a particularly close Jewish counterpart to the commentary's pain that does not end in death.

column5: fire not quenched night or day, smoke forever
column6: Isaiah's judgment-fire is not quenched by night or day and its smoke ascends forever; this gives the commentary's continually maintained fire a close Hebrew Bible formulation, even though Isaiah describes a devastated land.

column5: pit of torment and furnace of Gehenna opposite rest
column6: 4 Ezra reveals the pit of torment and furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest and paradise; this Jewish apocalyptic pairing illuminates the commentary's opposition between fire without relief and the full life of the other destination.

column5: prisoners gathered in pit and shut up
column6: Isaiah pictures rebels gathered like prisoners in a pit, shut in prison, and punished after many days; its sequence of capture, confinement, and delayed punishment parallels the commentary's entry into fire followed by an enduring state within it.

column5: book of life and lake of fire
column6: Revelation sends anyone absent from the book of life into the lake of fire; it joins exclusion from life to fiery judgment in the same way the commentary sets the denied life of 87:13 inside the fire.

column5: John's unquenchable fire and chaff
column6: John's own warning culminates in chaff burned with unquenchable fire; it brings the commentary's Yahya section into direct contact with its earlier fire and fading-vegetation imagery.

column5: fruitless tree, root, and fire
column6: John warns that every tree without good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire; this binds warning, failed living growth, root imagery, and fire more tightly than a merely verbal parallel.

column5: disobeying the Son, not seeing life, wrath remaining
column6: John contrasts present eternal life for belief with not seeing life and wrath remaining for disobedience; it closely matches the commentary's refusal of the life-giving call issuing in an abiding punitive condition.

column5: resurrection of life and resurrection of judgment
column6: Jesus distinguishes a resurrection of life from a resurrection of judgment; this gives a precise New Testament two-outcome horizon for the commentary's contrast between true postmortem life and the fire's condition.

column5: keeping the word and never seeing death
column6: Jesus promises that one who keeps his word will never see death; it is a positive inverse to 87:13, where absence of death is not blessed because it is detached from life and reception of the word.

column5: living believer will never die
column6: Jesus joins living and believing with never dying; this makes explicit the conjunction of deathlessness and life that the commentary says is present for the saved but denied in the fire.

column5: resurrection children cannot die anymore
column6: Those counted worthy of the resurrection cannot die anymore and are called children of God; this is a close positive counterpart to the commentary's distinction between immortal resurrection life and deathless punishment.

column5: obedience and entering rest
column6: Hebrews urges diligence to enter God's rest so that no one falls through the same disobedience; it links heeding versus refusal to rest, directly complementing the commentary's denial of rest in the fire.

column5: judgment fire consuming adversaries
column6: Hebrews describes deliberate rejection after knowledge as facing judgment and fire that consumes adversaries; it shares the warning-to-fire movement but contrasts with the commentary's fire that does not consume its victim into death.

column5: God's call refused, later cry unheard
column6: Zechariah states the exact reversal that people would not hear when God called, so God would not hear when they called; this strongly parallels the commentary's warning that rejected remembrance cannot later secure release.

column5: hear and the soul may live
column6: Isaiah calls hearers to incline the ear and hear so that their soul may live; it is a close Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's claim that answering the admonition is answering what gives life.

column5: life by every word from God's mouth
column6: Deuteronomy says a human lives by every word from YHWH's mouth rather than bread alone; it gives the commentary's life-giving reminder a concrete scriptural form beyond bodily nourishment.

column5: God kills and makes alive, none can deliver
column6: Moses attributes both killing and making alive to God and says none can deliver from his hand; it parallels the commentary's ordered death-life sequence while underscoring the impossibility of self-escape from final divine judgment.

column5: death swallowed forever and tears wiped
column6: Isaiah's promised victory swallows death forever and wipes tears away; it supplies the positive destination where death's removal means healed life, heightening the commentary's claim that the fire has no such life.

column5: loving present life loses it, preserving life eternal
column6: Jesus says that clinging to one's life in this world loses it, while relinquishing it preserves it for eternal life; this is a sharp Gospel analogue to the commentary's preferred near life versus the lasting life.

column5: perishing food and food abiding to eternal life
column6: Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food that remains for eternal life; it specifically supports the commentary's contrast of a short chosen worldly provision with a durable, real life.

column5: passing from death to life, remaining in death
column6: Love is said to mark passage from death to life, while lack of love leaves one in death; this offers another concrete Christian use of life and death as moral-spiritual states before final judgment.

column5: dwelling with devouring fire and everlasting burnings
column6: Isaiah's frightened sinners ask who can dwell with devouring fire and everlasting burnings; although its immediate setting is Zion's judgment, its language of inhabiting enduring fire closely meets the commentary's focus on remaining inside it.

column5: righteous dead enter peace and rest
column6: The upright person who dies enters peace and rests; this offers a prophetic positive counterpart to the commentary's secondary reading of death as stillness and rest, both withheld from the fire's inhabitant.

column5: seeking YHWH's word but not finding it
column6: Amos foresees people wandering in search of YHWH's word and not finding it; it gives a concrete prophetic form to the commentary's too-late remembrance after the time for hearing has passed.

column5: the living give thanks, unlike the dead
column6: Hezekiah says that the living, not the dead, give thanks to God; it clarifies the commentary's association of life with responsive remembrance and worship rather than bare continued sensation.

column5: the righteous dead are in peace
column6: Wisdom says that those who seemed to die are in peace; this Jewish reflection makes death a secure state for the righteous, a deliberate opposite to the fire where the sufferer receives neither death nor peace.

column5: no share in the world to come for denial of resurrection
column6: The Mishnah excludes from the world to come those who deny resurrection from the Torah and related fundamentals; this rabbinic rule concretely links rejection of revealed truth with loss of future life, as the commentary's warning logic does.

column5: John's moral exhortation and execution by Herod
column6: Josephus portrays John as exhorting justice and piety before Herod has him killed; this Jewish witness supplies historical narrative context for the commentary's righteous Yahya and distinguishes ordinary mortal death from the fire's deathless condition.

column4: Arabic Infancy Gospel, opening cradle-speech (chapter numbering varies)
column5: newborn Jesus speaks from the cradle
column6: The opening scene of the Arabic Infancy Gospel has the newborn Jesus speak from the cradle; its setting differs from the Qur'anic defense of Mary, but it is a specific Christian infancy parallel to the extraordinary cradle-speech invoked in the commentary.

column5: refusal to hear the prophet brings destruction
column6: Acts says that every person refusing to hear the promised prophet will be destroyed from the people; it shares the commentary's warning-and-refusal logic but uses destruction where 87:13 depicts an unended condition without death.

column5: no escape after neglecting salvation
column6: Hebrews asks how people can escape after neglecting such a great salvation; this concise warning formula parallels the commentary's closed possibility of escape after the reminder has been evaded.

column5: dead and alive again, lost and found
column6: The returning son is declared dead and alive again, lost and found; this recovery scene is a narrative positive counterpart to the commentary's moral death-life language and its final absence of a way back.
